title: Room Games
concept: After this one you can tell which room a trap is played in, and spot the good kind that does good for the people in it.
bookIdea: A good game is one whose social contribution outweighs the complexity of its motives, particularly when the player has come to terms with them. It contributes both to the well-being of the other players and to the unfolding of the one who is “it”. Since games rest on ulterior transactions, every game has some element of exploitation.

opener.setting: Friday, 9:05pm. Sam's birthday, apartment 3B. The speaker is on the shoe rack, a paper crown is on the fridge, and the cake has a dent in one corner already.

lines.text: “Careful with the cake, he's already spilt mango juice on my shoe. Twice.”
lines.cue: one foot up on the arm of the sofa, shoe in her hand

lines.text: “Eat something. Don't say you're full, you haven't touched the rice.”
lines.cue: a bowl in each hand, not sitting down

opener.ask: Work out which room each trap belongs to, and what makes the good kind different from the rest.

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Four rooms: the party, the clinic, the back room and the good kind. Tap the room the line belongs to.

items.text: “Oops, sorry, sorry! Have one on me, it's the least I can do.”
items.cue: a plastic cup in one hand, a napkin in the other
items.why: A spill with a sorry, and a drink offered as the cure. The room is full of people, and the apology is loud enough to win the forgiveness before anyone asks what the spill cost. That is the party.

traps.1: This would be the clinic if the talk were about a symptom and a plan for treatment. Here nobody is being treated. They are only being offered a drink.
traps.2: This would be the back room if the talk were about a plan to leave or to hide something. Nobody here is planning anything except another round.

items.example: A colleague's farewell lunch, Friday. The one who knocks over the cake says “Oops, sorry, have a slice,” and the table laughs before anyone asks who pays for the tablecloth.

items.text: “I can't do the stretch. The back's been bad for years, and you know what I'm like with it.”
items.cue: sitting on the edge of the bed, not lying down
items.why: A bad back is given as the reason before anything has been tried, and the bed is in a room where a stretch is the work. The excuse is accepted before the stretch even starts. That is the clinic.

traps.0: This would be the party if the back came up as a joke over a drink, and everyone laughed it off. Here it is a reason in a room with a bed and a physio waiting for an answer.
traps.2: This would be the good kind if the bad back were being turned into something useful for the people around him. Here it is only a reason to skip the work, and nobody is helped by it.

items.example: A driving instructor, Saturday. “My shoulder won't turn the wheel, so let's just sit here.” He writes “no lesson today” and the car stays in the car park.

items.text: “Omar's had his leaving papers in a drawer for two years. Every time they're ready, he finds a bug.”
items.cue: laughing, leaning over the cake plate
items.why: The papers are ready and the door is open, and the frightened Kid in him takes over and finds a bug just before the handover. The room is about getting out, and staying is what actually gets done.

traps.1: This would be the party if the talk were a joke about being late for a drink. The leaving papers are real, and the stopping is what matters.
traps.2: This would be the good kind if the bug were a gift to the team and the team grew because of it. Here nobody grows, and the papers stay in the drawer.

items.example: A cousin who has had a new-city job offer for a year. Each time the flat is ready to leave, the car needs a service first.

items.text: “Sit here, and I'll show you the formula. I like it when you can do it yourself. It makes me look good too, I'll admit that.”
items.cue: turning the laptop round so you can see the screen
items.why: Her reasons are mixed, and she says so. She likes looking clever, and she wants you to be able to do the work yourself. The help is real, and you come away able to do the formula alone, so the good outweighs the motive.

traps.0: This would be the party if the help were a joke about who is best at spreadsheets. Here she is teaching you a real formula, and the lesson is the point.
traps.1: This would be the clinic if she were treating you as someone who cannot cope. Nobody is being treated. She is handing over the formula.

items.example: A neighbour who shows you the water bill on her phone: “Watch me do it. I like knowing how, and I want you to know it too.”

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Three rooms. The same shape repeats in each one, so watch who is paying and who is getting the sorry.

items.title: Friday, 9:05pm, the birthday
items.setting: Apartment 3B, the living room, the cake on the coffee table. Sam is holding a glass of mango juice and a napkin. The Heckler, in your head: “Laugh it off, or you're the one who spoils the party.”

beats.text: “Oh no, sorry, sorry! My hand just... it's your new shirt. I'll pay for it, I swear.”
beats.cue: napkin in both hands, mango juice dripping off your sleeve

lines.text: “It's the new shirt, Sam. Pay for the dry cleaning on Monday, and say sorry to me, not to the room.”
lines.outcome: He goes red, says, “Monday, promise,” and looks at you properly for the first time all evening.
lines.why: A spill with a sorry is the spill and sorry: the apology is there to win your forgiveness before anyone names the cost. Naming the cost and asking for a date refuses to hand the forgiveness over for free, and it turns the sorry into a promise you can check.

lines.text: “It's fine, don't worry, it's only a shirt.”
lines.outcome: He cheers, and the room claps for the easy-going guest. Nobody mentions the shirt again.
lines.why: Kind, and it feels good for a second. The spill has been rewarded, and the next one is already on its way.

lines.text: “Sam, you ruin everything you touch.”
lines.outcome: He laughs too loudly, the room laughs with him, and you are the one who looks like the spoilsport.
lines.why: Attacking the spiller makes you the one who spoils the party. The spill and sorry gets the pity, and the blame lands on you.

beats.text: “Oh, he's always like this. Last week he knocked coffee over the printer. He's a menace.”
beats.cue: already cutting the cake, not looking up

lines.text: “Then he can pay for the printer as well. Sam, what are you paying for?”
lines.outcome: Sam's grin slips. “The printer,” he admits, “and the shirt. I'm on it.”
lines.why: You keep the cost in the room and ask the spiller to name it. Calling him a menace would be fun, but it would not make him pay.

lines.text: “He's a clown, what can you do?”
lines.outcome: Clara laughs and passes you the first slice, and the shirt stays wet.
lines.why: You agreed the spill is just who he is. That shrug is what the spill and sorry runs on.

lines.text: “Oh, he's only after attention. That's all he ever does.”
lines.outcome: Sam hears it from the kitchen, and the grin goes. He comes out with the jug and says nothing.
lines.why: You turned his spill into a bid for attention, and the room now feels sorry for him instead of asking what he owes.

beats.text: “Have one, go on. The cake's mango and the drinks are on me. Have one to say you're not angry.”
beats.cue: holding out a fresh glass, the paper crown tilted on his head

lines.text: “I'll take the cake, not the drink. And Monday is still Monday for the shirt.”
lines.outcome: “Cake it is,” he says, and cuts you the biggest slice. “Monday. Written down.”
lines.why: You separate the apology from the drink. The drink would settle the account without the shirt being paid, and you refuse that trade.

lines.text: “Okay, one, then.”
lines.outcome: He cheers, and the room cheers with him. The shirt is forgotten by the second song.
lines.why: The drink is the apology, and it comes as a treat. It closes the account without the dry cleaning.

beats.text: “Please, it's his birthday. Let the shirt wait, and let's eat the cake.”
beats.cue: the rice bowl in her arms, one eye on the spill

lines.text: “I'm fine with the birthday, Maya. The shirt is on Monday, and he knows which day.”
lines.outcome: Maya laughs and says, “Fine, but he gets the cake first.” Sam says, “Cake first, Monday after.”
lines.why: You keep the cost where it belongs and let the party go on. Holding a date is not the same as holding a grudge, and the date is the part that gets paid.

lines.text: “Fine, Maya, it's your flat.”
lines.outcome: Maya says, “Thank you,” and takes the rice to the kitchen. Nobody mentions the shirt.
lines.why: You gave the decision to the host. It keeps the peace for tonight and leaves the cost with you.

lines.text: “You always protect him, don't you? Every single time.”
lines.outcome: Maya goes still. “That's not fair,” she says, and the room goes back to its phones.
lines.why: You pointed the spotlight at the protector. The protector's chair is where you put her, and the cost is still unpaid.

items.payoff: Maya and Sam spend the rest of the party on the balcony, and you are left with the cake and the shirt. The dry cleaning is still unpaid, and nobody has said sorry to you properly.
items.example: A wedding caterer, Sunday. The waiter who drops the tray says “Sorry, sorry, have a sweet,” and the guests applaud before anyone mops the floor.

items.title: Wednesday, 6:15pm, the physio's room
items.setting: A clinic on the second floor near the bus stop. A bed with a paper sheet, a cracked poster of the spine, and a stool by the window. You came to keep Omar company. The Heckler, in your head: “Nobody can expect a man with a back like that to try.”

beats.text: “Lie back, Omar, and lift the left leg. Just the one, five times.”
beats.cue: one hand on the bed, the other on a clipboard

lines.text: “Omar, your back is bad. What's one thing you can do today, inside the pain?”
lines.outcome: Omar looks at the ceiling for a long time, then lifts the left foot a finger's width. “That much,” he says. “Count it.”
lines.why: The bad back is a real limit, and it is also the reason he gives for skipping everything. Asking what he can do inside the limit is a way of asking what he expects of himself. It keeps the back real without letting it become a pass.

lines.text: “Okay, the back's bad, let's skip the leg today.”
lines.outcome: The physio shrugs and writes “declined” on the form. Omar looks relieved, and the bed stays empty.
lines.why: You accepted the excuse as the whole story. The room goes quiet, and the back stays exactly where it was.

lines.text: “Your back's always bad when it suits you, Omar.”
lines.outcome: Omar gets off the bed, takes his jacket, and says the physio can't help him. The physio says nothing and writes it down.
lines.why: Calling the excuse a dodge invites a fight, and the fight becomes the reason to leave. A bad back can be challenged, but an insult in this room only gives him a way out.

beats.text: “Fine, one lift. But the bus home is going to be murder, so you can carry my bag.”
beats.cue: sitting up, rubbing the lower back

lines.text: “Then we write the one lift down, and you tell me how it feels tomorrow.”
lines.outcome: Omar nods. “Tomorrow, then. Properly.” The physio writes the date on the form.
lines.why: You count the small step and ask for a real report of the next day, not an argument about the bus. The back gets a plan with a date on it.

lines.text: “Sure, I'll carry your bag. Anything for a man with a back like that.”
lines.outcome: Omar laughs. The physio makes a note: friend to carry the bag.
lines.why: You accepted the excuse again, with a joke, and you have taken the bag. The back now has a helper, and the helper is you.

lines.text: “You've said that for three years, Omar. Nobody is stopping you.”
lines.outcome: Omar stares at you. “Well, I'll see you next week,” the physio says, and the session ends.
lines.why: You turned the excuse into a case against him. Now the session is about whether you are on his side, and the back drops out of the conversation.

beats.text: “Right, same time next week. What are you going to do between now and then, Omar?”
beats.cue: writing the next date on the card

lines.text: “Omar, you name the one thing, and I'll check on it with you next week.”
lines.outcome: Omar grins, a little sheepish. “Walk to the shop without the bag. Fine.”
lines.why: You hand the step back to Omar and offer a check-in, which is support, not a rescue. He sets the step himself, so the back becomes part of his plan.

lines.text: “Rest, I suppose, and I'll carry the bag again.”
lines.outcome: “Rest,” Omar says, and the physio's pen stops above the next date.
lines.why: Rest is a fair answer, but you offered the bag again. The week will be spent on the excuse, not on a step.

lines.text: “You'll never do it, Omar, so why bother booking?”
lines.outcome: The physio closes the card without writing the date, and Omar says, “Thanks for coming.”
lines.why: A trap move: you forecast his failure out loud. A prediction is a kind of verdict, and it gives him a reason to skip the next session.

items.payoff: Omar leaves with his jacket on and the form marked declined. The lift never happens, and the back is in exactly the state it was in before you came.
items.example: A gym trainer, Tuesday. “My knee won't bend past this, so let's just stand here.” The trainer nods and books the next session for the same excuse.

items.title: Thursday, 6:30pm, the glass room
items.setting: Halden, by the station, the fourth floor. The payments handover papers are on the table, and Daniel is tapping a pen. The Heckler, in your head: “Stay put. The papers can wait, and so can you.”

beats.text: “Payments can take you in January, if the migration is clean. The papers are on the table when you're ready.”

lines.text: “Good. I'll finish the migration by Wednesday and sign the papers the same day.”
lines.outcome: He nods once. “Wednesday. Good.” He slides the papers across.
lines.why: You name the date and the step, and you act on the offer you wanted. Getting out takes a decision on paper, not another month of good intentions.

lines.text: “Maybe. I'll see how the migration goes.”
lines.outcome: “See how it goes,” Daniel repeats, and the papers go back in the folder.
lines.why: A maybe leaves the door half open, and he closes it for you. Nothing is refused, and nothing is decided.

lines.text: “There's a bug in the import, so January is too soon. Maybe next year.”
lines.outcome: Daniel says, “Then we'll look at it together, and the papers stay here.” They stay in the drawer, and the bug stays unseen.
lines.why: You reached for a reason just as the door opened. The release is the thing you asked for, and the bug is the thing that keeps you in the room.

beats.text: “You've been so good all month. Ready to leave us? Payments will be lucky to get you.”
beats.cue: grinning, a spare pen in her hand

lines.text: “Yes, I'm ready. I'll hand you the notes on Monday, so you're not stuck with me.”
lines.outcome: Clara laughs. “Notes on Monday. You'd better mean it.”
lines.why: You say yes and name the handover, so the leaving has a date and a shape. The release is in your hands, not in the bug's.

lines.text: “Almost. Ask me again next week.”
lines.outcome: “Next week,” Clara says, and writes nothing on her pad.
lines.why: A delay with no date. The door stays ajar, and the week goes by in the same chair.

lines.text: “No. Nobody here will ever let me leave, will they?”
lines.outcome: Clara looks at you, then at Daniel, and says nothing. The papers stay in the folder.
lines.why: You turned the offer into a jail and made the others the guards. The scene ends with the papers still in the folder.

beats.text: “Show me the bug, then. If it's real, we'll fix it before the handover.”

lines.text: “There's one small bug, and it's logged. I'll fix it by Wednesday, and do the handover in January, not before.”
lines.outcome: Daniel turns the laptop back. “Wednesday, then. Put it in writing.”
lines.why: You name a real bug and a real date, and put the handover after both. The fix and the release are separate jobs, and you have named both.

lines.text: “I'll find it. Maybe it's in the old code.”
lines.outcome: “Find it by Wednesday,” he says. The bug is now a search with no end.
lines.why: Vague work keeps the release on hold. Nobody can say when the papers will move, including you.

lines.text: “You want me to find it for you, don't you? Like always.”
lines.outcome: Daniel closes the laptop. “Then January's on hold,” he says, and the papers go back in the folder.
lines.why: You handed him the job and ended the scene with a jab. The cost falls on the release, and the sting lands on the one who wanted to leave.

items.payoff: The papers go back in the folder, and the January move waits for another year. The bug is still in the import, and so are you.
items.example: A cousin planning a move to a new city, Sunday. She has the flat sorted and the bus ticket booked, then tells the family about a leaking tap that must be fixed first. The move waits another six months.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Two questions. Pick the explanation that fits what happened in the room.

items.text: Clara spends an hour on the formula and says she likes it when you can do it yourself, because it makes her look good too. Her reasons are mixed. What makes this the good kind?
options: Clara has no reasons of her own, so the help is pure.
The help is real and you can now do the formula yourself, even though her reasons are mixed.
Nobody can see her reasons, so the help counts as good.
items.why: Every trap has some hidden motive underneath. One earns the name good when what it gives the other people outweighs the tangle of motives, especially when the player has owned up to them, as Clara has. She helps you, and you leave able to do the work yourself.

traps.0: The book says every trap has some motive of its own, so pure help is not the test. Clara has reasons, and she names them out loud.
traps.2: This gets it the wrong way round. Clara's reasons are out in the open, and that is part of why the help counts as good. It leaves you able to do the work, and the motive has been owned.

items.example: A cousin at the tax desk, Sunday. “Sit here, I'll do the first page. I like being the clever one, but you'll finish the rest yourself.”

items.text: Omar has had his leaving papers ready for two years, and he finds a bug before every handover. Why does the bug keep him in the room?
items.cue: the papers still in the drawer
options: Because the bug is always real, so he has no choice but to stay.
Because the Kid in him dreads the outside, so it finds a reason to stay right before the door.
Because the others on the team will not let him leave.
items.why: The room is about getting out, and the frightened part of him can sabotage the release just before it happens. The bug is the excuse, and the dread is the reason. Fixing bugs will never end it, because the pattern needs the dread itself to be noticed.

traps.0: A real bug can be fixed in a week, yet the papers stay in the drawer for two years. The bug is the excuse, and the reason is somewhere else.
traps.2: The team would be glad to see him go, and would help with the handover. Nobody is holding him back, so the bug is coming from inside.

items.example: A friend who keeps promising to start the course in June. Each time the form is ready, the laptop needs a software update first.

debrief.nadia: Four rooms, and the same shape in each. Someone gets the sorry, the sigh, the bug or the favour, and the room lets them keep it. Ask who is paying in each room, and who gets the good of it.
debrief.bookNote: The books call these good games: a good game is one whose social contribution outweighs the complexity of its motives, particularly when the player has come to terms with them, so it helps the other players and the one who is “it”. The other rooms are party games (chapter 8), underworld games (chapter 10) and consulting-room games (chapter 11).

reflection.prompt: Which room did you spend the most time in this week, and what would the good kind of trap look like in that room?
